name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q01 - Basic chemical components of a nucleotide

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets correctly represents the three basic chemical components of a nucleotide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polymers of monomer units called nucleotides.

Step 2: Evaluation
Each nucleotide consists of three components: a nitrogenous base (purine or pyrimidine), a pentose sugar (ribose in RNA or deoxyribose in DNA), and a phosphate group. A nitrogenous base linked only to a pentose sugar forms a nucleoside, not a nucleotide.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The three components of a nucleotide are a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group.

answer.text: A nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a phosphate group
A nitrogenous base, a hexose sugar, and a phosphate group
An amino acid, a pentose sugar, and a sulfate group
A nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar, and a histone protein

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q02 - Pyrimidine nitrogenous bases in DNA and RNA

questiontext.text: Which nitrogenous base is found in RNA in place of thymine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nitrogenous bases in nucleic acids are classified into purines (adenine and guanine) and pyrimidines (cytosine, uracil, and thymine).

Step 2: Evaluation
Cytosine is common to both DNA and RNA. Thymine (5-methyl uracil) is present in DNA, whereas uracil is present in RNA at the place of thymine.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Uracil is found in RNA in place of thymine.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q03 - Hydrogen bonding between complementary base pairs

questiontext.text: In a double-stranded DNA molecule, how many hydrogen bonds are formed between Adenine and Thymine, and between Guanine and Cytosine, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the DNA double helix, nitrogenous bases on opposite strands pair specifically through hydrogen bonds.

Step 2: Evaluation
Adenine forms two hydrogen bonds with Thymine on the opposite strand, whereas Guanine is bonded with Cytosine through three hydrogen bonds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Adenine and Thymine form \(2\) hydrogen bonds, and Guanine and Cytosine form \(3\) hydrogen bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q04 - Pitch and base pair spacing of DNA double helix

questiontext.text: What is the pitch of a right-handed DNA double helix and the approximate distance between two consecutive base pairs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The two polynucleotide chains of DNA are coiled in a right-handed helical fashion with roughly \(10\text{ bp}\) per turn.

Step 2: Evaluation
The pitch of the helix (length of one complete turn) is \(3.4\text{ nm}\). Dividing \(3.4\text{ nm}\) by \(10\text{ bp}\) per turn gives an approximate distance of \(0.34\text{ nm}\) between two consecutive base pairs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pitch of the DNA double helix is \(3.4\text{ nm}\) and the distance between consecutive base pairs is approximately \(0.34\text{ nm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q05 - Central dogma of molecular biology

questiontext.text: Who proposed the Central dogma in molecular biology stating that genetic information flows from \(\text{DNA} \to \text{RNA} \to \text{Protein}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Central dogma describes the unidirectional flow of genetic information from DNA to mRNA (transcription) and from mRNA to protein (translation) in most organisms.

Step 2: Evaluation
Soon after the proposition of the DNA double-helix structure, Francis Crick proposed the Central dogma in molecular biology.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Francis Crick proposed the Central dogma in molecular biology.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q06 - Basic amino acids abundant in histones

questiontext.text: Histones carry a positive charge because they are rich in which two basic amino acid residues?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A protein acquires its net charge depending on the abundance of amino acid residues with charged side chains.

Step 2: Evaluation
Histones are positively charged basic proteins because they are rich in lysine and arginine residues, both of which carry positive charges on their side chains. This allows histones to bind tightly to negatively charged DNA.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Histones are rich in lysine and arginine.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q07 - Euchromatin versus heterochromatin properties

questiontext.text: In a typical eukaryotic nucleus, the region of chromatin that is loosely packed, stains light, and is transcriptionally active is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chromatin in the eukaryotic nucleus exists in two distinct packaging states with different staining intensities and transcriptional activities.

Step 2: Evaluation
Euchromatin is loosely packed, stains light, and is transcriptionally active. In contrast, heterochromatin is more densely packed, stains dark, and is transcriptionally inactive.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The loosely packed, lightly staining, transcriptionally active chromatin is euchromatin.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q08 - Griffith transforming principle bacterium

questiontext.text: In Frederick Griffith's 1928 transforming principle experiment, which organism was used and why did the S strain produce smooth shiny colonies?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Frederick Griffith investigated bacterial transformation using a pneumonia-causing bacterium that exhibits two distinct colony morphologies: smooth (S) and rough (R).

Step 2: Evaluation
The bacterium used was Streptococcus pneumoniae. The virulent S strain bacteria produce smooth shiny colonies because they possess a mucous (polysaccharide) coat, whereas the non-virulent R strain lacks this coat.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Griffith used Streptococcus pneumoniae, and the S strain produces smooth colonies because it has a mucous (polysaccharide) coat.

answer.text: Escherichia coli; presence of a protein capsule
Streptococcus pneumoniae; presence of a peptidoglycan cell wall only
Vicia faba; presence of a lipid coat
Streptococcus pneumoniae; presence of a mucous (polysaccharide) coat

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q09 - Stop codons and initiator codon in genetic code

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups correctly lists the three stop (terminator) codons in mRNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Out of the \(64\) triplet codons in the genetic code, \(61\) code for amino acids and \(3\) do not code for any amino acid, functioning instead as stop codons.

Step 2: Evaluation
The three stop terminator codons are UAA, UAG, and UGA. AUG codes for methionine and acts as the initiator codon, while UGG codes for tryptophan.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The three stop codons are UAA, UAG, and UGA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q10 - Secondary and actual compact structure of tRNA

questiontext.text: The secondary structure of tRNA looks like a ______, whereas in actual compact structure it looks like ______.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
tRNA acts as an adapter molecule that reads the genetic code via its anticodon loop and binds a specific amino acid at its acceptor end.

Step 2: Evaluation
In two-dimensional representations, the secondary structure of tRNA resembles a clover-leaf. In actual three-dimensional space, tRNA folds into a compact molecule that looks like an inverted L.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The secondary structure of tRNA looks like a clover-leaf, and its actual structure looks like an inverted L.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q11 - Chargaff rule calculation for base percentages

questiontext.text: If a double-stranded DNA molecule contains \(20\%\) cytosine, what is the percentage of adenine in that DNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The DNA molecule is double-stranded, and the percentage of cytosine (\(\text{C}\)) is \(20\%\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The DNA obeys standard Watson-Crick base pairing throughout its length.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Erwin Chargaff's rule for double-stranded DNA, \(\text{A} = \text{T}\) and \(\text{G} = \text{C}\), and the total percentage of all four bases is \(\%\text{A} + \%\text{T} + \%\text{G} + \%\text{C} = 100\%\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(\%\text{C} = 20\%\), we have \(\%\text{G} = 20\%\). Thus, \(\%\text{G} + \%\text{C} = 20\% + 20\% = 40\%\). The remaining percentage is \(\%\text{A} + \%\text{T} = 100\% - 40\% = 60\%\). Because \(\%\text{A} = \%\text{T}\), we obtain \(\%\text{A} = \frac{60\%}{2} = 30\%\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Summing all bases gives \(30\% + 30\% + 20\% + 20\% = 100\%\). Therefore, the percentage of adenine in the DNA is \(30\%\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q12 - Calculating base pairs from E. coli DNA length

questiontext.text: If the length of E. coli DNA is \(1.36\text{ mm}\), what is the approximate number of base pairs present in it? (Take the distance between two consecutive base pairs as \(0.34\text{ nm}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total length of DNA, \(L = 1.36\text{ mm}\). Distance between two consecutive base pairs, \(d = 0.34\text{ nm}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Convert both lengths into metres: \(1\text{ mm} = 10^{-3}\text{ m}\), so \(L = 1.36 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}\); and \(1\text{ nm} = 10^{-9}\text{ m}\), so \(d = 0.34 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m/bp}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total length of DNA helix \(L = \text{Number of base pairs } (N) \times d\), hence \(N = \frac{L}{d}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substituting the values: \(N = \frac{1.36 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}}{0.34 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m/bp}} = \frac{1.36}{0.34} \times 10^{-3 - (-9)}\text{ bp} = 4 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Multiplying back: \(4 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m/bp} = 1.36 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m} = 1.36\text{ mm}\). Thus, the number of base pairs is \(4 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q13 - Theoretical number of nucleosomes in mammalian cell

questiontext.text: A typical diploid mammalian cell has \(6.6 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\) of DNA, and a typical nucleosome contains \(200\text{ bp}\) of DNA helix. Theoretically, how many nucleosomes are present in a mammalian cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total diploid DNA content = \(6.6 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\). DNA per nucleosome = \(200\text{ bp}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Assume uniform wrapping of all genomic DNA into typical nucleosomes without extra linker variations.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Number of nucleosomes = \(\frac{\text{Total base pairs}}{\text{Base pairs per nucleosome}}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\(\text{Number of nucleosomes} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}}{200\text{ bp}} = \frac{6.6 \times 10^{9}}{2 \times 10^{2}} = 3.3 \times 10^{7}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking: \(3.3 \times 10^{7} \times 200 = 6.6 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\). Thus, there are theoretically \(3.3 \times 10^{7}\) nucleosomes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q14 - Enzyme inhibiting transformation in Avery MacLeod McCarty experiment

questiontext.text: In the biochemical characterisation of the transforming principle by Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty, digestion with which enzyme inhibited the transformation of live R cells into S cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty purified proteins, DNA, and RNA from heat-killed S cells and tested which macromolecule could transform live R cells into virulent S cells.

Step 2: Evaluation
They found that protein-digesting enzymes (proteases) and RNA-digesting enzymes (RNases) did not affect transformation, ruling out protein and RNA as the transforming substance. However, digestion with DNase inhibited transformation, proving that DNA caused the transformation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Digestion with DNase inhibited transformation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q15 - Radioactive isotopes used in Hershey and Chase experiment

questiontext.text: Why did Hershey and Chase use radioactive phosphorus (\(^{32}\text{P}\)) and radioactive sulfur (\(^{35}\text{S}\)) in their bacteriophage experiment?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
To determine whether viral protein or viral DNA entered E. coli during bacteriophage infection, Hershey and Chase needed isotopes that selectively label only one of the two macromolecules.

Step 2: Evaluation
DNA contains phosphorus (in its sugar-phosphate backbone) but lacks sulfur, so viruses grown on \(^{32}\text{P}\) had radioactive DNA but non-radioactive protein. Conversely, proteins contain sulfur (in sulfur-containing amino acids) but lack phosphorus, so viruses grown on \(^{35}\text{S}\) had radioactive protein capsules but non-radioactive DNA.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(^{32}\text{P}\) selectively labels DNA because DNA contains phosphorus but protein does not, whereas \(^{35}\text{S}\) selectively labels protein because protein contains sulfur but DNA does not.

answer.text: DNA contains sulfur but not phosphorus, whereas protein contains phosphorus but not sulfur
Both DNA and protein contain phosphorus and sulfur, but \(^{32}\text{P}\) is heavier than \(^{35}\text{S}\)
DNA contains phosphorus but not sulfur, whereas protein contains sulfur but not phosphorus
To label bacterial ribosomes with \(^{32}\text{P}\) and bacterial cell walls with \(^{35}\text{S}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q16 - Criteria for genetic material and failure of proteins

questiontext.text: Which criterion of a genetic material do proteins fail to fulfill right at the first step?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A molecule acting as genetic material must be able to replicate, be chemically and structurally stable, provide scope for slow mutations, and express itself as Mendelian characters.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because of base pairing and complementarity, both DNA and RNA can direct their own duplication (replication). Proteins lack complementary template-directed duplication and therefore fail to fulfill the very first criterion of generating their own replica.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Proteins fail to fulfill the criterion of being able to generate their own replica (replication).

answer.text: Containing nitrogen and carbon in their structure

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q17 - Evolution of DNA from RNA in the RNA world

questiontext.text: Why did DNA evolve from RNA as the predominant genetic material for storage of genetic information?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
RNA was the first genetic material and essential life processes evolved around it, but RNA also acted as a catalyst.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because RNA has a reactive \(2'\text{-OH}\) group and catalytic activity, it is labile, unstable, and mutates faster. DNA evolved from RNA with chemical modifications (deoxyribose lacking \(2'\text{-OH}\) and thymine in place of uracil) and a double-stranded structure with repair mechanisms, making it chemically less reactive and structurally more stable.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
DNA evolved from RNA because chemical modifications and double-stranded structure made DNA more stable and resistant to degradation and rapid mutation.

answer.text: Chemical modifications and double-stranded nature made DNA more stable and less reactive than RNA
DNA can directly code for protein synthesis without requiring any RNA intermediate
RNA cannot form complementary base pairs during duplication
DNA acts as a faster catalyst than RNA in metabolic reactions

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q18 - Rate and duration of DNA replication in E. coli

questiontext.text: Escherichia coli completes the replication of its \(4.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\) genome in \(18\text{ minutes}\). What is the approximate average rate of polymerisation by its DNA polymerase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA-dependent DNA polymerases in E. coli are highly efficient enzymes capable of polymerising a large number of nucleotides in a short time.

Step 2: Evaluation
Completing replication of \(4.6 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\) in \(18\text{ minutes}\) (\(1080\text{ seconds}\)) corresponds to an average rate of approximately \(2000\text{ bp per second}\) (accounting for bidirectional replication forks).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The approximate average rate of polymerisation is \(2000\text{ bp per second}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q19 - Dual role of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates in replication

questiontext.text: During DNA replication, deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) serve dual purposes by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA replication is an energetically expensive process requiring both building blocks (monomers) and chemical energy.

Step 2: Evaluation
Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates act as substrates for DNA polymerase and also provide energy for the polymerisation reaction because their two terminal phosphates are high-energy phosphates, similar to ATP.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates act as substrates and provide energy for polymerisation.

answer.text: Acting as enzymes and unwinding the DNA double helix
Forming RNA primers and sealing Okazaki fragments
Acting as substrates and providing energy for the polymerisation reaction

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q20 - Importance of origin of replication in vectors

questiontext.text: Why does a piece of foreign DNA require a vector to be propagated during recombinant DNA procedures?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA polymerases cannot initiate DNA replication on their own, nor does replication begin at random sites along a DNA molecule.

Step 2: Evaluation
Replication initiates at a definite DNA region termed the origin of replication. Because a foreign DNA fragment lacks an origin of replication recognised by the host machinery, it requires a vector that provides the origin of replication.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Vectors are required because they provide the origin of replication needed for propagation.

answer.text: Vectors supply deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates to the host cell
Vectors convert single-stranded DNA into double-stranded DNA
Vectors carry DNA ligase for joining the foreign fragment

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q21 - Polyploidy resulting from failure of cell division

questiontext.text: In eukaryotes, DNA replication takes place during the S-phase of the cell cycle. What chromosomal anomaly results if cell division fails to occur after DNA replication?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA replication and the cell division cycle must be tightly coordinated in eukaryotes to maintain constant ploidy across cell generations.

Step 2: Evaluation
If DNA replication completes during the S-phase but cell division fails to follow, the replicated chromosome sets remain within the same cell, resulting in polyploidy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Failure of cell division after DNA replication results in polyploidy.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q22 - Predicting mRNA sequence from coding strand

questiontext.text: If the sequence of the coding strand in a transcription unit is \(5'\text{-ATGCATGCATGC-3'}\), what will be the sequence of the transcribed mRNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Coding strand sequence = \(5'\text{-ATGCATGCATGC-3'}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The coding strand has \(5' \to 3'\) polarity, while the complementary template strand has \(3' \to 5'\) polarity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
RNA polymerase synthesises mRNA in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction complementary to the template strand. Consequently, the mRNA sequence is identical to the coding strand except that uracil (U) is present in place of thymine (T).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Replacing every T with U in \(5'\text{-ATGCATGCATGC-3'}\) gives \(5'\text{-AUGCAUGCAUGC-3'}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verifying via the template strand \(3'\text{-TACGTACGTACG-5'}\): complementary RNA is \(5'\text{-AUGCAUGCAUGC-3'}\). Thus, the mRNA sequence is \(5'\text{-AUGCAUGCAUGC-3'}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q23 - Exons, introns, and split genes in eukaryotes

questiontext.text: In eukaryotes, monocistronic structural genes have interrupted coding sequences. Which statement accurately distinguishes exons from introns?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Eukaryotic structural genes exhibit a split-gene arrangement in which coding sequences are interrupted by non-coding intervening sequences.

Step 2: Evaluation
Exons are the coding or expressed sequences that are retained and appear in the mature, processed mRNA. Introns are intervening sequences that are removed during RNA splicing and do not appear in mature or processed mRNA.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Exons appear in mature or processed RNA, whereas introns do not appear in mature or processed RNA.

answer.text: Introns appear in mature mRNA, whereas exons are removed during splicing
Both exons and introns are translated into polypeptides in eukaryotes
Exons appear in mature or processed RNA, whereas introns do not appear in mature or processed RNA
Exons are found only in prokaryotic polycistronic genes, whereas introns are found only in bacteria

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q24 - Role of sigma and rho factors in bacterial transcription

questiontext.text: In bacteria, RNA polymerase alone is only capable of catalysing elongation. It associates transiently with which factors to initiate and terminate transcription, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyses transcription of all RNA types in bacteria, but it requires accessory factors to alter its specificity for initiation and termination.

Step 2: Evaluation
Bacterial RNA polymerase associates transiently with the initiation factor sigma (\(\sigma\)) to bind the promoter and initiate transcription, and with the termination factor rho (\(\rho\)) to terminate transcription at the terminator region.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
RNA polymerase associates with sigma (\(\sigma\)) factor for initiation and rho (\(\rho\)) factor for termination.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q25 - Coupled transcription and translation in bacteria

questiontext.text: Why can transcription and translation be coupled in bacteria, often allowing translation to begin before mRNA is fully transcribed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Coupling of transcription and translation occurs when ribosomes attach to nascent mRNA while RNA polymerase is still transcribing it.

Step 2: Evaluation
In bacteria, two conditions permit coupling: first, bacterial mRNA does not require any processing (such as splicing) to become active; second, there is no separation of cytosol and nucleus, so both transcription and translation occur in the same compartment.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Transcription and translation can be coupled in bacteria because mRNA requires no processing and both processes occur in the same cellular compartment.

answer.text: Bacterial mRNA requires no processing to become active, and transcription and translation occur in the same compartment
Bacteria possess three specialised RNA polymerases that speed up translation
Bacterial mRNA contains introns that are spliced by ribosomes
Bacterial RNA polymerase directly synthesises polypeptides from DNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q26 - Division of labour among eukaryotic RNA polymerases

questiontext.text: Which set of RNAs is transcribed by RNA polymerase III in the eukaryotic nucleus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the eukaryotic nucleus, three RNA polymerases divide the transcription of different classes of RNA.

Step 2: Evaluation
RNA polymerase I transcribes \(28\text{S}\), \(18\text{S}\), and \(5.8\text{S}\) rRNAs. RNA polymerase II transcribes hnRNA (precursor of mRNA). RNA polymerase III is responsible for the transcription of tRNA, \(5\text{S rRNA}\), and snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA, \(5\text{S rRNA}\), and snRNAs.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q27 - Capping and tailing of eukaryotic hnRNA

questiontext.text: During post-transcriptional processing of eukaryotic hnRNA, what is added during capping at the \(5'\)-end and tailing at the \(3'\)-end?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In eukaryotes, primary transcripts (hnRNA) undergo splicing, capping, and tailing to form mature mRNA.

Step 2: Evaluation
In capping, an unusual nucleotide—methyl guanosine triphosphate—is added to the \(5'\)-end of hnRNA. In tailing, \(200\text{–}300\) adenylate residues are added at the \(3'\)-end in a template-independent manner.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Methyl guanosine triphosphate is added at the \(5'\)-end (capping), and \(200\text{–}300\) adenylate residues are added at the \(3'\)-end (tailing).

answer.text: Poly-A tail at \(5'\)-end; methyl guanosine triphosphate at \(3'\)-end
Methyl guanosine triphosphate at \(5'\)-end; \(200\text{–}300\) adenylate residues at \(3'\)-end

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q28 - Point mutation causing sickle cell anemia

questiontext.text: Sickle cell anemia is a classical example of a point mutation involving a single base pair change in the gene for the beta-globin chain. Which amino acid substitution does this mutation cause?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A point mutation is a change of a single base pair in DNA that can alter a single codon in mRNA and substitute one amino acid in the resulting polypeptide.

Step 2: Evaluation
In sickle cell anemia, a single base pair change in the beta-globin gene results in the substitution of the amino acid residue glutamate with valine.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The mutation causes the substitution of glutamate to valine.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q29 - Location and function of untranslated regions in mRNA

questiontext.text: Where are untranslated regions (UTRs) located in an mRNA molecule, and what is their role?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A translational unit in mRNA is flanked by the start codon (AUG) and a stop codon, but the mRNA molecule also carries additional sequences outside this coding region.

Step 2: Evaluation
Untranslated regions (UTRs) are present at both the \(5'\)-end (before the start codon) and the \(3'\)-end (after the stop codon). Although they are not translated into amino acids, they are required for an efficient translation process.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
UTRs are present at both the \(5'\)-end before the start codon and the \(3'\)-end after the stop codon, and are required for efficient translation.

answer.text: At both \(5'\)-end (before start codon) and \(3'\)-end (after stop codon); required for efficient translation
Between exons within the coding region; removed during translation
Only at the \(3'\)-end after the stop codon; required for DNA replication
Only at the \(5'\)-end before the start codon; code for the signal peptide

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q30 - Levels of gene expression regulation in eukaryotes

questiontext.text: In eukaryotes, regulation of gene expression can be exerted at all of the following levels EXCEPT:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gene expression ultimately results in the formation of a polypeptide, and eukaryotes can regulate this pathway at multiple checkpoints from DNA to protein.

Step 2: Evaluation
In eukaryotes, regulation may occur at four levels: transcriptional level (formation of primary transcript), processing level (regulation of splicing), transport of mRNA from nucleus to cytoplasm, and translational level. Amino acid synthesis in the Golgi apparatus is not a level of gene expression regulation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Regulation of gene expression in eukaryotes does not occur at the level of amino acid synthesis in the Golgi apparatus.

answer.text: Amino acid synthesis in the Golgi apparatus
Transport of mRNA from nucleus to cytoplasm

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q31 - Basal expression of lac operon for lactose entry

questiontext.text: Why must a very low level of expression of the lac operon be present in E. coli cells all the time, even in the absence of lactose?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lactose acts as the inducer of the lac operon by entering the bacterial cell and inactivating the repressor protein.

Step 2: Evaluation
Lactose cannot diffuse freely into the cell; it requires the membrane protein permease (encoded by the \(y\) gene) to be transported into the cell. Therefore, a basal, very low level of lac operon expression is needed continuously so that enough permease is present to transport lactose inside when it becomes available.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A very low basal expression is required so that permease is present to allow lactose to enter the cells.

answer.text: To prevent the \(i\) gene from synthesising repressor protein
To convert glucose into allolactose inside the cell
Otherwise lactose cannot enter the cells via permease to induce the operon
To allow RNA polymerase to bind to the operator region

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q32 - Scale and bioinformatics of Human Genome Project

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the estimated cost and scale of the Human Genome Project (HGP) at its inception?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Human Genome Project was termed a mega project because of the enormous size of the human genome (approximately \(3 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\)), its cost, and its data storage demands.

Step 2: Evaluation
At an estimated sequencing cost of US \(\$3\) per bp, the total estimated cost was approximately \(9\text{ billion US dollars}\). Storing the sequence in typed books of \(1000\) pages each with \(1000\) letters per page would require \(3300\) books for a single human cell, necessitating high-speed computation and the new discipline of Bioinformatics.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The estimated cost was approximately \(9\text{ billion US dollars}\), and storing the sequence would require \(3300\) books of \(1000\) pages each with \(1000\) letters per page.

answer.text: Estimated cost of \(9\text{ million US dollars}\); \(330\) books required
Estimated cost of \(3\text{ billion US dollars}\); \(33,000\) books required
Estimated cost of \(9\text{ billion US dollars}\); \(330\) books required
Estimated cost of \(9\text{ billion US dollars}\); \(3300\) books required

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q33 - Gene counts on human chromosome 1 and Y chromosome

questiontext.text: According to the Human Genome Project, which human chromosome was the last to be completely sequenced (in May 2006) and has the most genes, and which chromosome has the fewest genes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Out of the \(24\) human chromosomes (\(22\) autosomes, X, and Y), gene density varies widely across chromosomes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Chromosome 1 was the last human chromosome to be completely sequenced (in May 2006) and contains the highest number of genes (\(2968\)). The Y chromosome has the fewest genes (\(231\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Chromosome 1 has the most genes (\(2968\)) and was sequenced last, while the Y chromosome has the fewest genes (\(231\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q34 - Definition of DNA polymorphism in human populations

questiontext.text: Traditionally, an allelic sequence variation at a locus is described as a DNA polymorphism if more than one variant (allele) occurs in the human population with a frequency greater than:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
DNA polymorphism refers to inheritable genetic variation observed at a high frequency in a population, arising from germ-cell mutations that accumulate over generations.

Step 2: Evaluation
By definition, an allelic sequence variation is termed a DNA polymorphism if more than one variant (allele) at a locus occurs in the human population with a frequency greater than \(0.01\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The threshold frequency is greater than \(0.01\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q35 - Meselson and Stahl DNA proportions after 80 minutes

questiontext.text: In Meselson and Stahl's experiment, E. coli cells with completely heavy DNA (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)) were transferred to a light medium (\(^{14}\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\)) and allowed to grow for \(80\text{ minutes}\). What would be the proportions of light (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)) and hybrid (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)) DNA molecules after \(80\text{ minutes}\)? (Generation time of E. coli = \(20\text{ minutes}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial DNA: \(100\%\) heavy (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{15}\text{N}\)). Growth medium after transfer: \(^{14}\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\). Total growth duration = \(80\text{ minutes}\). Generation time = \(20\text{ minutes}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
DNA replicates semiconservatively, so the two original \(^{15}\text{N}\) parental strands remain intact and each always pairs with a newly synthesised \(^{14}\text{N}\) strand.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Number of generations \(n = \frac{\text{Total time}}{\text{Generation time}}\). Total DNA molecules after \(n\) generations per initial molecule = \(2^n\). Number of hybrid molecules remains constant at \(2\) (one per original heavy strand).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Number of generations \(n = \frac{80\text{ min}}{20\text{ min}} = 4\). Total DNA molecules produced from \(1\) initial molecule = \(2^4 = 16\). Out of these \(16\) molecules, \(2\) are hybrid (\(^{15}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)) and \(16 - 2 = 14\) are light (\(^{14}\text{N}/^{14}\text{N}\)). Converting to percentages: light DNA = \(\frac{14}{16} \times 100\% = 87.5\%\), and hybrid DNA = \(\frac{2}{16} \times 100\% = 12.5\%\) (a ratio of \(7:1\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(87.5\% + 12.5\% = 100\%\). Thus, the proportions are \(87.5\%\) light DNA and \(12.5\%\) hybrid DNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q36 - Calculating base sequence differences between humans

questiontext.text: Assuming the haploid human genome contains \(3 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\) and \(99.9\%\) of the nucleotide base sequence is identical among all humans, in approximately how many base pairs would two individuals differ?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Genome size = \(3 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp}\). Percentage similarity = \(99.9\%\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The remaining percentage accounts for the base pair differences between two individuals.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Percentage difference = \(100\% - 99.9\% = 0.1\%\). Number of differing base pairs = \(\frac{0.1}{100} \times \text{Total bp}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\(\text{Number of differences} = \frac{0.1}{100} \times 3 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp} = 10^{-3} \times 3 \times 10^{9}\text{ bp} = 3 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(3 \times 10^{6}\) is \(0.1\%\) of \(3 \times 10^{9}\). Thus, two individuals would differ in approximately \(3 \times 10^{6}\text{ bp}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q37 - Distinguishing nitrogenous bases, nucleosides, and linkages

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly identifies a set containing ONLY nucleosides and the bond linking the sugar to the base in them?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A nucleoside consists of a nitrogenous base linked to a pentose sugar, without any phosphate group.

Step 2: Evaluation
Adenine, thymine, uracil, and cytosine are free nitrogenous bases. Cytidine, guanosine, uridine, and deoxythymidine are nucleosides. In every nucleoside, the nitrogenous base is linked to the OH of \(1'\text{C}\) of the pentose sugar via an N-glycosidic linkage.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cytidine, guanosine, and deoxythymidine are nucleosides formed via an N-glycosidic linkage.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q38 - Statement-based analysis of DNA double-helix stability

questiontext.text:
Consider the following two statements regarding the double-helix structure of DNA:
Statement I: The two polynucleotide chains have anti-parallel polarity and are coiled in a left-handed fashion.
Statement II: In addition to hydrogen bonds, the stacking of the plane of one base pair over the other confers stability to the helical structure.
Which of the following is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Watson and Crick's double-helix model specifies both the handedness of coiling and the forces stabilising the helix.

Step 2: Evaluation
The first statement is incorrect because although the two chains have anti-parallel polarity (\(5' \to 3'\) and \(3' \to 5'\)), they are coiled in a right-handed fashion, not a left-handed fashion. The second statement is correct because the plane of one base pair stacks over the other in the double helix, which, in addition to hydrogen bonds, confers stability to the helical structure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first statement is incorrect, and the second statement is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q39 - Identifying incorrect observation in Hershey-Chase experiment

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about the Hershey and Chase (1952) experiment is INCORRECT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the Hershey-Chase experiment, bacteriophages with \(^{32}\text{P}\)-labelled DNA or \(^{35}\text{S}\)-labelled protein coats infected E. coli, followed by blending and centrifugation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Viral coats were removed by agitating in a blender and separated by centrifugation. Bacteria infected with \(^{32}\text{P}\)-labelled phages showed radioactivity in the bacterial pellet (cells) and not in the supernatant, proving DNA entered the bacteria. Conversely, bacteria infected with \(^{35}\text{S}\)-labelled phages showed no radioactivity in the bacterial cells; instead, radioactivity was detected in the supernatant containing the empty viral protein coats. Claiming that \(^{35}\text{S}\) radioactivity was detected inside bacterial cells is therefore false.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The incorrect statement is that bacteria infected with \(^{35}\text{S}\)-labelled phages showed radioactivity inside the cells.

answer.text: Blending was used to remove the viral coats from the bacterial surface
Bacteria infected with \(^{35}\text{S}\)-labelled phages showed radioactivity inside the bacterial cells
Centrifugation separated the heavier infected bacterial cells from the lighter viral particles in the supernatant

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q40 - Deducing mRNA from template strand given in 5' to 3' direction

questiontext.text: A template strand of DNA has the nucleotide sequence \(5'\text{-GCTTAGCGA-3'}\). What will be the sequence of the mRNA molecule transcribed from this template strand?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Template strand sequence = \(5'\text{-GCTTAGCGA-3'}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The transcribed mRNA must be antiparallel and complementary to the template strand, with RNA polymerase synthesising mRNA in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Base-pairing rules for transcription: DNA \(\text{G} \to \text{RNA C}\), DNA \(\text{C} \to \text{RNA G}\), DNA \(\text{T} \to \text{RNA A}\), and DNA \(\text{A} \to \text{RNA U}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
First, write the template strand in the \(3' \to 5'\) direction by reversing it: \(3'\text{-AGCGATTCG-5'}\). Now write the complementary mRNA in the \(5' \to 3'\) direction: \(\text{A} \to \text{U}\), \(\text{G} \to \text{C}\), \(\text{C} \to \text{G}\), \(\text{G} \to \text{C}\), \(\text{A} \to \text{U}\), \(\text{T} \to \text{A}\), \(\text{T} \to \text{A}\), \(\text{C} \to \text{G}\), \(\text{G} \to \text{C}\). This yields \(5'\text{-UCGCUAAGC-3'}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Reading the complement directly from \(5'\text{-GCTTAGCGA-3'}\) gives \(3'\text{-CGAAUCGCU-5'}\), which when written \(5' \to 3'\) is \(5'\text{-UCGCUAAGC-3'}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q41 - Exceptions and features of the genetic code

questiontext.text: All of the following statements about the genetic code are true EXCEPT:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The genetic code has specific universal and structural properties, including triplet codons, degeneracy, contiguous reading, and initiation/termination signals.

Step 2: Evaluation
Codons are read in mRNA in a contiguous fashion without punctuations. AUG has dual functions (methionine and initiation). The code is nearly universal, with exceptions found in mitochondrial codons and some protozoans. However, there are NO tRNAs for stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA); instead, release factors bind to stop codons during termination.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The false statement is that specific tRNAs exist for stop codons.

answer.text: Specific tRNAs with complementary anticodons exist for each of the three stop codons
The codon is read in mRNA in a contiguous fashion without any punctuations
Exceptions to the universality of the genetic code occur in mitochondrial codons and some protozoans
AUG codes for methionine and also functions as an initiator codon

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q42 - Comparing frameshift mutations with three-base insertions

questiontext.text: If a coding sequence of mRNA is read as triplets, what is the consequence of inserting two bases at a single site versus inserting three bases together at that same site?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because the genetic code is a non-overlapping triplet read contiguously without punctuations, altering the number of nucleotides affects the grouping of downstream codons.

Step 2: Evaluation
Inserting two bases shifts the reading frame for every subsequent codon from the point of insertion (a frameshift insertion mutation), altering all downstream amino acids. Inserting three bases together adds one complete codon (and one amino acid) while keeping the downstream reading frame completely unaltered.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Inserting two bases causes a frameshift altering all downstream codons, whereas inserting three bases adds one codon and leaves the downstream reading frame unaltered.

answer.text: Both insertions cause a frameshift that alters all downstream amino acids
Inserting two bases shifts the reading frame downstream, whereas inserting three bases adds one codon without altering the downstream reading frame
Inserting two bases leaves the reading frame unaltered, whereas inserting three bases shifts the reading frame
Neither insertion affects the amino acid sequence because the genetic code is degenerate

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q43 - Structure and catalytic role of ribosome in translation

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the structure and catalytic role of the ribosome during translation in bacteria?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The ribosome is the cellular factory for protein synthesis, composed of structural RNAs and about \(80\) different proteins, existing as a large subunit and a small subunit in its inactive state.

Step 2: Evaluation
Translation begins when the small subunit encounters an mRNA. The large subunit contains two sites where subsequent aminoacyl-tRNAs bind close enough for peptide bond formation. Furthermore, the ribosome itself acts as a catalyst: \(23\text{S rRNA}\) in bacteria functions as a ribozyme (RNA enzyme) to catalyse peptide bond formation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The large subunit provides two sites for aminoacyl-tRNAs, and \(23\text{S rRNA}\) acts as a ribozyme catalysing peptide bond formation.

answer.text: The small subunit contains the catalytic \(23\text{S rRNA}\) ribozyme and two tRNA binding sites
The ribosome consists exclusively of proteins and requires external DNA polymerase to form peptide bonds
The large subunit has two sites for subsequent aminoacyl-tRNAs, and \(23\text{S rRNA}\) acts as a ribozyme for peptide bond formation
The large subunit encounters mRNA first, and \(18\text{S rRNA}\) catalyses peptide bond formation in bacteria

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q44 - Why the lac operon shuts down after lactose addition

questiontext.text: In a medium where E. coli is growing, lactose is added, which induces the lac operon. Why does the lac operon shut down some time after the addition of lactose?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Regulation of the lac operon is an example of regulation of enzyme synthesis by its substrate (lactose).

Step 2: Evaluation
When lactose is added, it acts as an inducer, inactivating the repressor and allowing transcription of \(\beta\)-galactosidase, permease, and transacetylase. \(\beta\)-galactosidase hydrolyses lactose into glucose and galactose. Once all available lactose is consumed, the repressor is no longer inactivated (since glucose and galactose cannot act as inducers), so the repressor binds back to the operator and shuts down the operon.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The lac operon shuts down because all the lactose is hydrolysed into glucose and galactose, which cannot act as inducers, allowing the repressor to bind the operator again.

answer.text: Because the \(i\) gene stops synthesising repressor protein after lactose is added
Because galactose acts as a co-repressor that permanently mutates the operator
Because lactose is hydrolysed into glucose and galactose, which cannot act as inducers, so the repressor re-binds the operator

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q45 - Statement-based analysis of HGP methodologies

questiontext.text:
Consider the following two statements regarding the methodologies of the Human Genome Project:
Statement I: Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs) focused on identifying all genes that are expressed as RNA, whereas Sequence Annotation involved sequencing the whole genome (coding and non-coding) and assigning functions later.
Statement II: The fragments were sequenced using automated DNA sequencers based on a method developed by Frederick Sanger.
Which of the following is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Human Genome Project combined two complementary sequencing strategies with automated sequencing technology.

Step 2: Evaluation
The first statement is correct: ESTs targeted only genes expressed as RNA, while Sequence Annotation took the blind approach of sequencing the entire genome (both coding and non-coding regions) and annotating functions afterwards. The second statement is also correct: cloned DNA fragments in BAC/YAC vectors were sequenced using automated DNA sequencers working on the principle developed by Frederick Sanger.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both statements are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q46 - Incorrect salient feature of the human genome

questiontext.text: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding the salient observations drawn from the Human Genome Project?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
HGP revealed the exact base-pair count, estimated gene number, coding fraction, and functional annotation status of the human genome.

Step 2: Evaluation
The human genome contains \(3164.7\text{ million bp}\), the average gene consists of \(3000\text{ bases}\), and the functions of over \(50\%\) of discovered genes remain unknown. However, the total number of genes is estimated at about \(30,000\)—much lower than earlier estimates of \(80,000\) to \(1,40,000\). Stating that the human genome contains \(80,000\) to \(1,40,000\) genes is therefore incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The incorrect observation is that the total number of genes in the human genome is estimated at \(80,000\) to \(1,40,000\).

answer.text: The total number of genes in the human genome is estimated at \(80,000\) to \(1,40,000\)
The functions are unknown for over \(50\%\) of the discovered genes
Less than \(2\%\) of the genome codes for proteins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q47 - Satellite DNA separation and polymorphism accumulation

questiontext.text: Why is DNA polymorphism observed at a higher probability in non-coding repetitive (satellite) DNA sequences than in protein-coding sequences?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Satellite DNA forms small peaks separated from bulk genomic DNA during density gradient centrifugation and shows high polymorphism.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mutations in non-coding repetitive sequences generally do not have any immediate impact on an individual's reproductive ability. Consequently, germ-cell mutations in these regions are not eliminated by natural selection and keep accumulating generation after generation, generating high DNA polymorphism.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mutations in non-coding DNA sequences may not immediately affect reproductive ability and therefore accumulate across generations.

answer.text: Non-coding DNA replicates using RNA polymerase, which makes more errors
Satellite DNA is located only in somatic cells and never enters germ cells
Mutations in non-coding sequences may not immediately impair reproductive ability and thus accumulate over generations
Satellite DNA lacks hydrogen bonds between complementary bases

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MCQ_Q48 - Characteristics and sensitivity of VNTR in DNA fingerprinting

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR) in DNA fingerprinting is INCORRECT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
VNTR belongs to the mini-satellite class of satellite DNA, where a small sequence is arranged tandemly in variable copy numbers across chromosomes.

Step 2: Evaluation
VNTR size varies from \(0.1\) to \(20\text{ kb}\), and PCR increases the sensitivity of DNA fingerprinting so that DNA from a single cell is sufficient. Furthermore, DNA from every tissue of an individual (blood, hair follicle, skin, saliva, sperm) shows the exact same degree of polymorphism. Therefore, claiming that VNTR banding patterns differ between blood and saliva of the same individual is incorrect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The incorrect statement is that VNTR banding patterns differ between blood and saliva cells of the same individual.

answer.text: VNTR belongs to a class of satellite DNA referred to as mini-satellite
The size of VNTR varies from \(0.1\) to \(20\text{ kb}\)
Using PCR, DNA from a single cell is sufficient to perform DNA fingerprinting
VNTR banding patterns differ between blood cells and saliva cells of the same individual
